missing.text: No first aid manual written for the public: the IFRC guidelines are written for trainers, and the national guides have only a few first aid pages each.
The IFRC guidelines name no emergency number; 112 and the national numbers come from the national civil-protection guides.
No simple method for sorting many injured people (triage) written for the public.
Some medicines the IFRC guidelines name, such as aspirin, adrenaline or an inhaler, may be given only where local rules allow; no source here gives those rules for any country.

disagree.text: Cooling a burn: the IFRC guidelines say cool running water for at least ten minutes, ideally twenty, but not ice-cold; the Austrian guide says to rinse with lukewarm water and to stop if the person shivers.

missing.text: No guide to caring for a sick person at home over days or weeks.
Nothing on long-term illness without a doctor (diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease), on pregnancy and birth, or on teeth.
No guide to medicines: what to take for what, doses, or how long medicines keep.
Helplines are named only for Germany, Styria in Austria, and Poland.
No guide for water that may hold fuel, chemicals or sewage, beyond the WHO note that treating water at home does not remove chemicals.
Nothing on finding water outdoors (springs, streams, rain) or on how safe a river or lake is to drink from.
No boil-water notice from a water utility, and nothing on how long taps keep running in a tall building during a blackout.
No source compares water tablets or filters; one Austrian guide names a single brand.

disagree.text: How much water to keep: the German guide says 2 litres a person a day (half a litre for cooking); the Swiss leaflets at least 9 litres a person, enough to drink and cook for three days; the Austrian supplies guide 1.5 litres to drink plus 3.5 for washing a day, and seven 1.5-litre bottles a person; the French national guide 6 litres a person for its 72-hour kit; the Polish government guide at least 3 litres a person a day, and the Polish RCB guide 14 litres a person for a week; the WHO note 2.5 to 3 litres a day to drink and eat, and 7.5 to 15 in all. Each page states its own figure.

Sun disinfection (SODIS): the WHO note says about a day of sun near the equator, two if it is cloudy; the Austrian supplies guide says about 6 hours of full sun, about three days under cloud, and that it kills 30 to 80 per cent of germs.

missing.text: No food-safety guide from a health authority on what to throw away after a long power cut or a flood; the rules here come from civil-protection leaflets.
Nothing on how long fridge and freezer food stays safe without power, beyond eating perishable food first and keeping the doors shut.
No guide to cooking over a fire or on a grill beyond the warning that grills and camping stoves belong outside.

disagree.text: How long to plan for: 72 hours (the French national guide), at least 3 days (the Polish government guide), about a week (the Swiss leaflets, the Austrian supplies guide and the Polish RCB guide), 10 days if possible and at least 3 (the German guide), one to two weeks (the Styrian blackout guide), at least 10 to 14 days (the Austrian blackout checklist).
Cooking on a grill in a blackout: the Austrian guides suggest a garden grill without saying where to use it; the German guide says grills and camping stoves are for outdoors only.
How often to check the stock: once a year (the Austrian supplies guide and the French easy-to-read guide), twice a year (the French national guide), every few months (the Polish government guide).

missing.text: No manual for generators or portable power stations: only the warnings in this guide.
Nothing for people in tall buildings beyond checking the lift: water pressure, long stairs, neighbours who cannot get down.
No guide to medical devices that need power, such as oxygen or breathing machines, beyond asking for help early.

disagree.text: How long to prepare for a blackout: at least 10 to 14 days (the Austrian blackout checklist), one to two weeks (the Styrian blackout guide), 10 days (the German guide), about a week (the Swiss leaflet); for any crisis, 72 hours (the French national guide) or at least 3 days (the Polish government guide).

missing.text: Little on heat waves at home: the Spanish guide on adverse weather gives general advice and the IFRC guidelines cover cooling a person down; nothing on keeping rooms cool.
No guide to judging whether a building damaged by an earthquake, a storm or a fire is safe to stay in.
Little on public shelters (a section of the Polish government guide), and nothing on sheltering outdoors.
Little on an emergency toilet: the Polish government guide describes a plastic bag on a bucket, put into a separate container after use; nothing on getting rid of the waste safely.
Nothing on keeping clean with very little water, beyond when to wash hands.
No guide to cleaning a home after sewage or flood water got in.
Nothing on stopping an illness such as diarrhoea spreading in a household.
Storms, hail and strong winds: only the Spanish guide on adverse weather, a few lines in the French national guide, and an Austrian page on thunderstorms in the mountains.
No guide to landslides, or to avalanches beyond rescue among mountaineers.
No guide to cleaning up and drying a home after a flood.
On chemical and nuclear accidents, only where to shelter, the iodine warning, and in the Polish RCB guide how long to stay inside (at least 24 hours): nothing on cleaning up.

Each hazard's pages are written for one country (Italy, Germany, Austria, France, Spain or Poland), with its own numbers and alerts; sirens and alert systems are explained for Italy, Germany, Austria, France and Poland.

disagree.text: Escaping through smoke: the German guide says never to; the Spanish self-protection guide says that if you must go out through smoke, breathe through a damp cloth and crawl.

missing.text: No guide to radios for talking to each other, such as PMR walkie-talkies, CB or amateur radio; the Polish government guide only lists them among things to have.
A family crisis plan is only in the Polish government guide; the French national guide says to agree with relatives how to stay in touch.
Warning systems are explained only for Germany, Austria, Italy, France and Poland.
No guide to reading a map or using a compass.
No guide to growing food: soil, planting times for European climates, staple crops such as potatoes and beans, or watering.
No guide to saving seed, or to growing in pots or on a balcony.
No guide to preserving food at home: bottling in jars, drying, pickling, fermenting or freezing.
No guide to telling whether home-preserved food is safe to eat.
No guide to hand tools, sharpening or a basic tool kit.
No guide to repairs in the home (taps, toilets, windows, simple electrical work) or to small engines.
No guide to batteries, power banks or portable power stations.
No guide to solar panels or other home power systems.
No generator manual: the power guide has only the warnings that the civil-protection leaflets give.
No hazard maps (floods, earthquakes, landslides) for any area.
Nothing on finding water in nature (springs, wells, rain), or on wild plants and mushrooms.
Nothing on reading a map or using a compass.
